title: NEC tests parking tech that only starts charging once you exit your car
teaser: Japan's new parking tech charges drivers only upon exit—a shift facilitated by AI that raises questions about the future of urban surveillance.
summary: Japan’s NEC is pioneering new parking technology that charges drivers only once they exit their vehicle, utilizing AI and real-time video analysis. This system raises concerns about potential surveillance capitalism while offering safety benefits. Other tech developments include Fujifilm preparing for a partial spin-off of its printer division amid market shifts. Meanwhile, China's Envision commissioned a massive 2GW+ datacenter in Inner Mongolia, providing one million PFLOPS of AI power. Additionally, Infosys secured a decade-long contract to modernize Crocs’ systems, and Australia has launched an inquiry into the privacy implications of smart glasses.
content: SOFTWARE NEC tests parking tech that only starts charging once you exit your car PLUS: Infosys to wear Crocs for a decade; Fujifilm may quit printers; 2GW datacenter debuts in western China; and more! ASIA IN BRIEF Japan's NEC has started tests of parking technology that will start charging once a driver leaves their car. Most car parks record the time a driver enters the facility and start charging, or depleting a free parking period, at that moment. That means drivers pay for time spent driving around looking for a spot and for the time it takes to exit a car park. NEC, in concert with another Japanese company called UrbanChain, will next month test a system that detects when a driver pulls up in a parking spot and exits their car - and starts charging for parking at that moment. That's only possible using cameras and AI analysis of real-time video, and the tests NEC will conduct in September will investigate how many cameras are needed to make its plans feasible. NEC's announcement also mentions "data utilization services targeting commercial facilities that can be used for monitoring vehicle occupant exit counts, analyzing facility visitor trends, and more" plus "new possibilities for data utilization." Which sounds like a new form of surveillance capitalism, brought to car parks. The two companies also think there's a safety benefit to their proposal, as it can spot drivers who haven't left their cars for an extended period - a potential sign of illness. They also hypothesize that if drivers know they won't be charged while searching for a spot or exiting a center, they may drive more safely. Fujifilm may join Japan's printer exodus Fujifilm last week informed investors [PDF] that it is investigating a partial spin-off of its printer business. The company wants to float the business and retain up to 20 percent of its shares; an idea it thinks will mean Fujifilm can focus on its other businesses. If the plan goes ahead, Fujifilm will join fellow Japanese printer-makers Epson . Toshiba, and Ricoh in reducing its exposure to the biz. It's not hard to see why Fujifilm is eyeing the exit: Analyst firm IDC recently said "a confluence of structural transformation and cyclical pressure" has brought uncertainty and sharply falling sales to the printer market. 2GW-plus datacenter opens in western China Chinese company Envision last week announced the commissioning of a two-gigawatt-plus datacenter in Ulana, Inner Mongolia. The company said the 120,000-square-meter facility can house up to one million GPUs and deliver one million PFLOPS of AI computing power. Renewable energy powers the facility, which is located in China's west - making it an expression of Beijing's Data East, Compute West plan that calls for construction of large datacenters closer to sources of clean energy and away from large population centers. Cable operator calls for police probe after faults follow "suspicious" activity Australian submarine cable operator and entrepreneur Bevan Slattery on Sunday claimed "some suspicious/coincidental activity" took place at the time two of his cables experienced a fault. "This is a concerning development. Partially because submarine cables are the digital lifeblood of our nation, but also because this could very well turn out to be the second such incidence in a Federally declared cable protection zone," Slattery wrote. His post includes a marine chart that shows a vessel called the GEM Sapphire, which ship-tracking site VesselFinder lists as a 183-meter long tanker, repeatedly crossing the path of two cables. Infosys to wear Crocs for ten years Indian tech services giant will spend the next decade making sure the world's ugliest shoes can be produced efficiently, after scoring a deal to help Crocs modernize its systems. Infosys says it will "unify data across the organization and aim to empower Crocs, Inc. with real-time, insight-driven decision-making - accelerating innovation while enhancing efficiency, responsiveness and customer experience." Apparently, the deal "help Crocs, Inc. address key industry challenges, including rising costs, inconsistent processes and the need for increased agility. The transformation will standardize operations and aim to enable the business to better respond to evolving consumer and market demands." There's no mention if the deal will mean anyone looks cool wearing Crocs. Maybe even a decade of help from Infosys can't make that possible. Australia urges smart glasses privacy probe Australian discount department store Kmart last week started selling low-end smart glasses for just AU$89 ($62/£46). The Guardian reported they sold out swiftly, sparking a privacy debate that quickly saw Australia's Attorney-General write to the nation's Privacy Commissioner to ask "that this issue be given priority consideration." "Privacy is an essential part of all our lives," said Attorney-General Michelle Rowland, before citing "widespread community concerns about the potential impacts of 'smart glasses', particularly for women and children." ®

title: Demoralized developer's desperate hack came back to haunt him on LinkedIn
teaser: A developer's 'terrible idea' to trick Python 3 into thinking it was still Python 2 allowed a company to delay necessary system fixes for years.
summary: In a nostalgic piece titled 'Who, Me?', developer Walter recounts his desperate hack during a complex migration from Python 2 to Python 3. After staffing cuts reduced morale, fixing stubborn system issues proved impossible. Walter's fix involved creating a symbolic link (`ln -s /usr/bin/python2 /usr/bin/python3`), essentially tricking the systems into thinking the old language was still active. This ingenious workaround kept operations running smoothly for years. However, this temporary solution was eventually found and corrected by another coworker during the final Linux upgrade, highlighting the persistence of technical debt.
content: Software Demoralized developer's desperate hack came back to haunt him on LinkedIn A script that shouldn't have worked, on a project that never ended, for a company that hardly cared WHO, ME? The past may be a foreign country, but it's one The Register likes to explore each Friday in "Who, Me?" - our reader-contributed column that shares your tales of workplace mistakes and great escapes. This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Walter," who once worked for one half of a duopoly competing in the intertwined markets for bad poetry celebrating memorable life moments and questionable television dramatizing the sentiments in those poems. The duopoly didn't make for a stable industry. "We produced a steady cycle of layoffs and hiring," Walter lamented. He nonetheless survived the latest round of layoffs and found himself upgrading systems from Python 2 to Python 3. "Our vendors had stopped pretending Python 2 was still a reasonable life choice," he told The Register . That move coincided with an upgrade to a new version of Linux that happily ran Python 3. "The older one technically could too, but only after a series of rituals involving symbolic links, configuration tweaks, and what I can only describe as informed superstition. It worked on about 80 percent of our systems and the remaining 20 percent flatly refused to cooperate for reasons nobody could explain." Walter told us he blamed the problem on a recent change of vendor in the office cafeteria. "It fit the evidence about as well as anything else," he wrote. Everyone on the team knew the upgrade-resistant 20 percent had to be fixed, but the recent redundancies had left morale so low that nobody was willing to pull the necessary all-nighters. The fact that some of the staff had decided to drink their way through the situation didn't help either. "One morning, fueled by spectacularly bad coffee and the news that a job interview had been pushed back another week, I had what can only be described as a terrible idea," Walter admitted. "What if I simply pointed Python 3 at Python 2?" He tried it by adding the following symbolic link to a script: ln -s /usr/bin/python2 /usr/bin/python3 "I expected fire. Or alarms. Or at least one very concerned email," he told The Register . "Instead... it worked. Not 'mostly worked.' It worked well enough that nothing complained, nothing paged us, and nobody noticed." Walter celebrated his success by leaving the following comment in the configuration script: "Yeah, yeah, yeah. I know, I know. At least I was mostly sober so it can't be THAT dumb!" Eight years later, Walter had thankfully moved on to another job, although he still checked LinkedIn occasionally. During one visit to Microsoft's bottomless trove of B2B sales advice, he spotted a message from one of the remaining workers at the poetry/television company. The survivor reported that the last Linux upgrade was finally complete. "They'd also finally found the symbolic link, after it survived a move from a script to Ansible," Walter told Who, Me? Has a moment of exasperation or desperation come back to haunt you? If so, don't get frustrated: click here to share your story with Who, Me? Our mailbag has seen better days, so fresh contributions are especially welcome. ®

title: Google Play adds Venmo as a payment option
teaser: Google Play now accepts Venmo! This major payment addition makes digital content even easier to buy amid massive market spending ($167B+ by 2025).
summary:
Google Play is expanding its payment ecosystem by integrating Venmo, allowing users to pay for games, apps, subscriptions, and digital content using Venmo's wallet or linked bank/card methods. This addition enhances the convenience of making in-app purchases across various content-based apps.

Users can link Venmo through their account settings, joining existing options like PayPal, Cash App, and major cards (Amex, Visa, etc.) already available in the U.S. The move comes amid massive growth in digital consumption; Sensor Tower reported that user spend on both iOS and Play Store was projected to exceed $167 billion for in-app purchases in 2025, marking a 10.6% increase year-over-year.
author: Ivan Mehta
content: Google said that it is adding Venmo as a payment option today on Google Play for purchases including games, apps, add-ons, and other digital content. The company said that users can use Venmo's wallet or other linked payment methods, such as bank accounts and cards, to pay for subscriptions or tip creators within different content-based apps. Users can go to payment methods within their account's settings to link a Venmo account. Google Play already offers other digital payment methods including PayPal and Cash App along with cards from American Express, Visa, Mastercard, Discover, and JCB in the United States. Outside the U.S., the company has also experimented with allowing users to pay for digital purchases using cash at a nearby store. People are spending more money on apps and games across the world. In 2025, user spend across iOS and Play Store was over $167 billion for in-app purchases, up 10.6% year-on-year, according to a report from analytics firm Sensor Tower.

title: This great retro-inspired keyboard now comes preassembled
teaser: The NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition delivers a stunning retro look with high-end components preassembled for just $189.
summary: For those who desire the look of a retro mechanical keyboard without the daunting task of assembly, the NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition offers convenience at $189. This wired, tenkeyless board features a gasket-mounted construction and hot-swap MX switches for excellent tactile feel. It comes preassembled with high-quality components including benchmark GMK CYL Classic Beige keycaps and tuned TypePlus stabilizers. Available in earthy tones like clay or lichen, this model makes enthusiast-grade performance accessible to professional users who want quality without the DIY commitment.
author: Nathan Edwards
content: You probably know just by looking at it if the Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is for you. Do you want a retro-looking wired keyboard without a number pad? Great. Do you care that it doesn't have wireless? Perfect. Do you want it preassembled? Buddy, you're in the right place. But Nathan, you might say, preassembled is the regular way to buy a keyboard . That is the baseline expectation. Most people buying a cake expect a cake, not a box of cake mix. And that's true, for most people and most keyboards. But until now, the Classic-TKL has only been available as a bare-bones kit, and now you can buy one ready to go, with quality components, for less than the price of doing a similar build yourself. If you're like me, figuring out what keycaps, switches, and stabilizers to use, then putting them all together, is a big part of the fun of mechanical keyboards. But if you just want something to type with that looks retro and sounds and feels nice, without having to build it yourself - or if you were going to use classic beige keycaps anyway - then the Underscore Edition might be up your alley. $189 The Good Great retro beige aesthetic Fully remappable High-quality components Hot-swap sockets Great sound and feel The Bad Only one keycap option, only one switch option Wired only No extra keycaps The $189 NovelKeys Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a wired-only, gasket-mounted tenkeyless mechanical keyboard. It has an injection-molded plastic case with a high forehead, reminiscent of the 18-year-old Realforce 86U , and a silicone mat on the base for sound dampening. It also has hot-swap MX switches, full RGB backlighting, and a light bar (both of which can be turned off), and it's fully programmable using the Via web app. The Classic-TKL has been around for a couple of years in kit form. I built one and wrote about it in 2024 ; I also tested the glow-in-the-dark version . I like them a lot! But apparently not everyone who wants a nice retro-looking keyboard also wants a craft project. Michael Sickler, who owns NovelKeys, told me that the Underscore Edition is aimed at giving NovelKeys' keyboard enthusiast customer base something they can recommend to friends and family. It's also aimed at professionals who might lurk on the keyboard subreddits and Discords enough to know what they want, but don't want to build it themselves. (This is basically the same thing Ryan Norbauer told me about his Seneca , except the Seneca is 20 times more expensive.) From the top: boulder, lichen, and clay. I tested the clay but look at that green. Photo: NovelKeys The Underscore Edition comes in clay (warm beige), boulder (taupe-ish), and lichen (a dusty green). My review unit is clay, but I'd buy the lichen personally. It ships with NovelKeys' own Classic Blue switches , GMK CYL Classic Beige keycaps , a USB A-to-C cable, and preinstalled and pretuned TypePlus stabilizers . These are name-brand parts. GMK CYL keycaps are the benchmark for doubleshot Cherry-profile keycaps. They're several steps in quality above the keycaps that come with a Keychron, for example. The letters and numbers are crisp and clear and the consistency is unmatched. They're also expensive; you'd pay at least $120 if you bought them on their own , though you would get more keycaps. The Classic-TKL comes with just the ones you need to cover the board. Nice thick doubleshot keycaps and smooth switches. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge The TypePlus stabilizers are also a good choice; I've installed and tuned a couple sets myself, but the people who made them do a better job. There's no rattle or tick on any of the stabilized keys. And the Classic Blue linear switches (also made by TypePlus) are also nice. They're smooth and stable, with almost no wobble; at 53g actuation force and 63g bottom-out, they're medium-heavy, like a lighter version of the Cherry MX Blacks in my first-ever mechanical keyboard in 2009. They're not silent, but they're also not as loud as you'd expect a keyboard this beige to be. (I still feel like a blue switch should be clicky, though.) I try to avoid the "fans of the genre" review. You know, "if this is the kind of thing you like, you're going to like it." But once you get past the strictly utilitarian, pretty much everything about mechanical keyboards comes down to preference and taste. The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is a well-executed version of what it is. If you want an earth-tone retro-looking tenkeyless board - a classic TKL, if you will - with linear switches and beige Cherry-profile keycaps, it's a great choice. It has a nice side profile. Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge When you think of it as a high-quality preassembled version of an enthusiast DIY keyboard, with name-brand parts, it's also a good deal. I built the DIY version of the same board with the same stabilizers and similarly priced keycaps in September 2024. It worked out to $276, and took me an hour to put together (most of which was spent lubing and tuning the stabilizers). The Underscore Edition costs $189, $100 more than the bare-bones kit. You can't get keycaps, switches, and stabilizers of this quality for $100 combined. But it's also true that $189 can get you a lot of keyboard these days, especially if you're not attached to the Classic-TKL's particular vibe. Even within the tenkeyless form factor, the Evoworks Evo80 costs $169 and comes with an aluminum case and both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless. Same for the $179 Wobkey Crush 80 . But those are different keyboards, with different aesthetics. The 8BitDo Retro 87 is closer, with several classic-computing-inspired flavors including Commodore 64 and IBM Model M , for around $100. But - no disrespect to the 8BitDo here - those look maybe a smidge more casual than the Classic-TKL. I prefer the Classic-TKL's plastic chassis to the aluminum of the Evoworks or Wobkey boards. But I wouldn't mind if it had wireless. It'd also be nice if it shipped with a few extra keycaps, in case you want Mac legends or Control in its proper place (Caps Lock). While I'm being picky: I also wish it came with the option for MTNU Classic Beige keycaps, rather than just CYL, because I like MTNU better. An electrocapacitive switch option would be nice too, but now I'm just getting greedy. (Actually, now I'm just reinventing the Realforce .) If you want the Classic-TKL in a different color, or with different switches or keycaps, there's still the kit version and the Glo version. And if you want a different keyboard entirely, well, those abound. The Classic-TKL Underscore Edition is the thing that it is, and it's good at that. I'd still go for the green one, though. title: Keychron’s wireless Hall effect keyboard is back to its lowest price
teaser: Get customizable Hall effect sensors for less: Keychron's K2 HE keyboard is on sale at Amazon for $103.99.
summary:
Keychron has dropped its aluminum-clad K2 HE 75-percent wireless Hall effect keyboard price to $103.99 (from $130) on Amazon. This affordable device offers advanced customization and features, including support for open source QMK firmware flashing and hot-swappable switches.

Furthermore, the keyboard supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing users to customize everything from actuation points to key bindings via Keychron's web tool.
author: Cameron Faulkner
content: Getting a keyboard with customizable Hall effect sensors is more affordable than it used to be, and you don't need to compromise on quality to get a good deal. Keychron's aluminum-clad K2 HE with a 75-percent layout is down to $103.99 (was $130) at Amazon , which matches the lowest price we've seen occur a few times throughout the year. The option with wood siding is $111.99 at Amazon , also 20 percent off its original price. The keyboard can connect via USB-C, or wirelessly via Bluetooth or with a more reliable 2.4GHz connection. Its key bindings, actuation points, and much more can be configured in Keychron's web-based tool. Or, you can flash your own firmware to the keyboard thanks to its open source QMK support. In case you haven't owned a Hall effect keyboard before, they're worth considering if you've wanted more granular control over how much (or how little) effort is needed to press a key. What's more, the sensors support Rapid Trigger, which primes each switch for another input long before it has been fully released, possibly letting you get the jump on opponents. The switches are hot-swappable, and the keyboard natively supports Windows, macOS, and Linux. This is a nice-looking keyboard for the money.

title: Clicks’ Power Keyboard brings BlackBerry-style typing to any phone — with some compromises
teaser: Clicks revived the BlackBerry experience with a $99 Power Keyboard, bringing tactile typing back to modern phones via MagSafe.
summary: Clicks Technology has released the $99 Power Keyboard, a slide-out accessory designed for smartphone users who miss physical typing experiences reminiscent of BlackBerrys. The keyboard is MagSafe-compatible and built with a 2,150 mAh internal battery that also supports wireless charging (MagSafe/Qi2). Functionally impressive, it allows deep customization, enabling actions like linking Apple Shortcuts or setting up custom number row shortcuts. However, the review notes significant compromises in portability and bulkiness when attached to larger phones. While excellent for power users who want an alternative to on-screen keyboards, its versatility extends beyond phones, allowing pairing with devices such as tablets, Smart TVs, and AR/VR headsets.
author: Sarah Perez
content: Clicks Technology , the startup determined to bring back physical keyboards to smartphones, began shipping its now-$99 MagSafe-compatible Power Keyboard this summer, after some delays . As of last week, 75% of the pre-orders from the first batch had shipped to customers. Designed to work with a range of devices, this new, slide-out keyboard with tactile buttons can accommodate different phone sizes and can be used in either portrait or landscape mode, the company says, giving any phone a BlackBerry-like feel. The device is something of a teaser for what's to come when Clicks ships its first smartphone, the BlackBerry-like Clicks Communicator , also featuring a physical keyboard, later this year. Like the upcoming smartphone, the idea behind the Power Keyboard is to provide an alternative to onscreen keyboards for those who miss the speed and reliability that came with typing on a small, physical keyboard. However, in its current implementation, the Power Keyboard suffers from the same fate as the company's earlier Clicks keyboard - a smartphone case that included a physical keyboard. It can make the phone feel top-heavy and difficult to hold in portrait mode, especially if you're using a larger smartphone as I did in tests with the iPhone 17 Pro Max and Pixel 10 XL. Still, the device itself is crafted with care, and could appeal to those who still desperately long for their BlackBerry. Image Credits: Clicks Technology Unboxing the device, we noticed the Power Keyboard was nicely packaged as a premium device would be, with peel-away cling films to prevent scratches during shipping and a full-color Quick Start guide to using the product. You may first need to charge the device's battery via USB-C, though we found ours shipped with a charge already. To pair the device with your phone over Bluetooth, press and hold the power button and slide out the keyboard. We quickly paired the device with our Android phone. We ran into trouble once we switched over to the iPhone. Even after "forgetting" the device on Android, it still refused to pair with our iPhone. Returning to the instructions, it appears this was our mistake. The trick is to press a number key alongside the power button on the keyboard to add a second Bluetooth device. (The only way to actually "forget" a device is by removing it from its slot using the Clicks mobile app.) The keyboard attaches to your phone via MagSafe or Qi2. If your phone doesn't support either technology, you could opt to use an adhesive ring or a phone case that adds the magnetic power profile instead. Image Credits: Clicks Technology Once connected, you can then pull the keyboard out when you need to type. Helpfully, the keyboard adjusts to different phone sizes, so it will work with standard models as well as larger "Ultra" or "Pro Max" devices. We appreciated the satisfying clicks as the keyboard locked into place on the various sliders. The keyboard offers an adjustable LED backlight, so you can type in the dark. The keys themselves have a nice, clicky feel and are well-placed, making them easy to reach. While it takes quite a bit of adjustment after years of on-screen keyboards to return to pressing buttons, the learning curve is less steep than it was on the earlier Clicks keyboard case. It's clear that the company has been iterating on what it learned with its older device, and those lessons have been channeled into this product. In addition, while Clicks' older keyboard case pulled power from the phone by way of its USB-C connection, the Power Keyboard instead includes a built-in 2,150 mAh battery. Image Credits: Clicks Technology The product itself has a slimmer profile than some snap-on battery packs, at 119.7 × 76.6 × 15.2mm, and doesn't add an unreasonable amount of weight at 180 grams. Nevertheless, this is not something that would fit well in a woman's pants pocket. The keyboard could get caught on a back pocket as well, as it could slide open if you press against the device while trying to cram the phone and keyboard into your pocket too quickly. Despite the added heft, there is an advantage to the battery pack that powers the keyboard - it can provide wireless charging to products with MagSafe and Qi2. (You can opt to entirely disable wireless charging in the Clicks companion app, if you prefer to keep all the power reserved for the keyboard itself. Or you can designate a portion of the battery just for the keyboard.) Another key advantage of the Power Keyboard is that it is highly customizable. Users can enable the Clicks key on the keyboard to function as a Tab button, or turn on "Cursor Mode" (Sym + CMD) to make certain letters on your keypad work as directional keys that move a cursor on the screen. Image Credits: Clicks Technology You can also adjust various settings like the idle timeout, battery reserves for wireless charging, LED backlight, and whether the Return key works as a hard or soft return. You can create your own Number Row shortcuts that allow you to press a number and the Sym button to enable Esc, volume controls, play/pause options, page up/down, and more. And you can pair Apple Shortcuts with certain keys to do other things like start a call, get a weather forecast, turn on the flashlight, receive an AirDrop, send texts, and much more. (Several popular shortcuts are included in the Clicks app, but you can add your own.) These, of course, are power user features that you'll only appreciate if you get comfortable with typing on the keyboard first. That could take some time to learn, and arguably, you'll be more comfortable using smaller, standard phones or lightweight options, like the iPhone Air. As for larger devices, we found it much easier to get started in landscape mode. Image Credits: Clicks' mobile app We also struggled to type comfortably with our iPhone case on, although it's a heftier, protective case, not a slim case. To test the device, we removed the case and used our iPhone bare. While that was much better, it was still somewhat difficult to use because of the larger phone. The company itself says it has tested the device with a number of phone models, including the iPhone Air, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, 16 Pro, Pixel 9, Galaxy Fold, and other Android devices. Whether or not the keyboard is worth the purchase has much to do with how much you really miss your BlackBerry; for the time being, it's an affordable enough holdover until the company's smartphone ships, at least. (Prototypes of the phone were much easier to use when we tried them at CES in January. It's obviously easier to make a comfortable device when Clicks is in control of all the technical specifications, instead of having to create something that works with phones of various weights and sizes.) While the Power Keyboard works as advertised, for the sake of comfort and portability, I'd prefer to make the switch to physical keys with Clicks' Communicator smartphone. Image Credits: Clicks Technology If you also decide this keyboard is not for you, all is not lost: There's still another way to use the product. Because the Power Keyboard should be able to pair with any device that supports external Bluetooth keyboards, you could use it with tablets, smart TVs like the Apple TV, or AR/VR headsets, like the Apple Vision Pro. This could come in handy when you're trying to set up new apps and have to type your email address and passwords awkwardly via a remote control or other input method. TechCrunch tries new devices via review units, which are later returned to the company or donated, depending on the company's specific return procedures.

title: Jeff Bezos might finally get his hands on a sports team
teaser: Jeff Bezos is reportedly targeting Liverpool FC for $1.8 billion, joining a wave of American billionaires seizing stakes in U.K. soccer teams.
summary:
Jeff Bezos is reportedly aiming to acquire a substantial stake (at least 30%) in Liverpool FC for approximately $1.8 billion. This potential investment marks his debut in sports ownership. The trend of American billionaires investing in U.K. football, exemplified by rivals owning stakes in multiple Premier League clubs, suggests that English soccer is an attractive high-profile asset market.

Beyond the stadium, Bezos's interest signals broader business ambitions; his AI company, Prometheus, also plans to set up shop in London's King's Cross AI hub. The reported deal places a mega yacht and professional sports team in the modern billionaire portfolio playbook.
author: Dominic-Madori Davis
content: Jeff Bezos is reportedly attempting to join the club of very rich Americans buying stakes in U.K. soccer teams. Bezos, alongside others including Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin, is looking to buy at least a 30% stake in the English soccer team Liverpool at a £1.35 billion valuation (around $1.8 billion), The Guardian reports . If the deal closes, it will be the first sports investment for the billionaire, although he reportedly previously looked at buying a stake in a U.S. football team. Liverpool is one of the most notable sports teams in Europe and is worth about $6 billion, reports Forbes. Arguably, this team has the kind of brand recognition in the U.K. as the Dallas Cowboys has in the U.S. It seems no billionaire portfolio is complete these days without a mega yacht and a sports team, so Bezos' interest is not surprising. There's also something very romantic these days about owning an English soccer team after the success of TV shows like "Ted Lasso" and Ryan Reynolds' FX show "Welcome to Wrexham" about his experience owning that English team. Other American billionaires in this club include Todd Boehly and Mark Walters (who also own the LA Dodgers and LA Lakers) buying Chelsea; New York Jets co-owner (and former U.S. Ambassador to the U.K.) Woody Johnson buying Crystal Palace; Dan Friedkin taking a stake in Everton; and Bill Foley leading a group that also included Michael B. Jordan buying Bournemouth. For that matter, owning a stake in a U.K. sports team has also become a celebrity cultural phenom. Besides Reynolds and Jordan, Tom Brady purchased a minority stake in Birmingham City. Will Ferrell has a minority stake in Leeds United, alongside Russell Westbrook and Michael Phelps. Liverpool is one of the top names in English football Image Credits: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista / Getty Images Sky Sports had a story earlier this year mapping out why so many Americans seem to be taking over U.K. football. It found that 13 out of 20 Premier League clubs (the top football league in England) had American shareholders. Soccer has become increasingly popular in the U.S., and many of the top sports franchises, like the NFL and MLB, are either too expensive or closed off to new buyers. It's much more possible to buy into a Premier League team. Owning a share in such a team also buys access and proximity to some of the most bankable and recognizable sports icons on Earth. Bezos over the past few years - especially since he married former news anchor and TV show host Lauren Sánchez - has become seen as more of a cultural figure, rather than solely a tech mogul. So, with a net worth currently sitting at around $280 billion , perhaps it's actually more than time that Bezos got himself a sports team. Amazon has also streamed some European soccer leagues in the past - and Bezos has growing interests in the U.K. As we previously reported, his new AI company Prometheus is reportedly looking to sign a lease to move into London's AI hub King's Cross.

title: Bluesky now lets you hide reposts from that annoying person you follow
teaser: Bluesky added a feature letting users hide unwanted reposts from specific accounts, giving more control over their feed.
summary: Bluesky has rolled out a user-requested feature allowing users to hide reposts from specific individuals in their feeds, preventing unwanted content clutter. To activate this privacy control, one simply navigates to the person’s profile and selects 'Hide reposts in feeds.' Additionally, Bluesky is testing a beta feature that will automatically display post numbers within long threads. This utility aims to help users gauge the length of discussions without manual counting and can be toggled on via settings.
author: Jay Peters
content: Bluesky has added a new feature that lets you hide reposts from a specific person in your feeds. The tool might be helpful if you want to stop seeing reposts from that one person who clogs up your feed with reposts of things you don't care about. If you follow me, I may be that person, I'm sorry. I try not to be. You can hide reposts from individual users by going to their profile, clicking the three dots button, and selecting the option to "Hide reposts in feeds." (X offers a similar toggle.) Bluesky also says that it's launching a beta feature that will automatically add post numbers to threads. For long threads, it could be a useful way to get a sense of how much there might be to read, and it means you won't have to manually add the numbers yourself. (Meta's Threads already adds post counts to threads .) You can turn the feature on from Bluesky's settings.

title: Anker’s travel charger works in almost any country and is down to $20
teaser: Keep all your gadgets charged worldwide with Anker's compact adapter, covering over 200 countries—all for under $20!
summary: For international travelers, the Anker Nano Travel Adapter offers versatile charging for multiple gadgets. It can simultaneously charge up to five devices using its combination of two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, and a standard AC outlet. The adapter is marketed as compatible with over 200 countries/regions and is highly compact. While one USB-C port provides 20W—suitable for phones and tablets—the device cannot charge most laptops directly via its USB ports. Crucially, users must note that the Nano does not convert voltage; travelers must verify their electronics (like hair dryers) support the destination's voltage before use.
author: Sheena Vasani
content: If you've got international travel coming up, an adapter is essential for keeping your phone, earbuds, power banks, and other gadgets charged. Anker's Nano Travel Adapter is one of our picks from our guide to the best gadgets for summer travel because it can charge up to five devices at once, yet it's small enough to fit in the palm of your hand. It's also available in black for just $19.99 ($6 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , and directly from Anker (with code WS7DV2BNB82J ) matching its best price to date. The Nano's four built-in sets of prongs should keep you covered in "over 200 countries and regions," according to Anker. It also features two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports, along with an AC outlet for plugging in a standard wall charger. A single USB-C port delivers up to 20W, which should be enough to get an iPhone 17 to 50 percent in less than 30 minutes. That's not enough power to charge most laptops, making the USB ports better suited for smaller gadgets like phones, tablets, earbuds, and power banks. You can still charge your laptop, however, by plugging its wall charger into the AC outlet. What's more, it's designed to take up as little space as possible. The adapter's only an inch thick with its prongs folded in and, at 3.8 ounces, weighs less than a smartphone. Just keep in mind that the Nano doesn't convert voltage, so you'll want to make sure gadgets like hair dryers and electric razors support the voltage at your destination before plugging them in.
